lines: At one time the Leader of Men
was staying in a mountain cave
This is what was reasoned out [then]
who was dwelling in that city,
the great theras of great renown;
and the therīs with great powers:[^w2]
traceless like the flame of a lamp.
While the World’s Lord still is living,
I’ll travel that peaceful path too.”
she foresaw the end of her life.
would be destroyed that very day,
she set out from her own ashram,
carrying her robe and her bowl.
at the wheel-marked [soles of his feet],
sitting off to one side [of him,]
she spoke these words to the Teacher:
the last of old age has arrived;
I’m reporting to the Great Sage:
Old age has ripened for me [now];
Giving all you up I will go:
my refuge is made in myself.
In the final days of old age,
Where there’s no birth, no growing old,
nor sickness and death, O Great Sage,
the Lord of Sages[^w8] [then] said this:
“What better can I say to you,
be cut off for all assemblies.”[^w10]
Having heard the words of the Sage,
in the home I was your chief queen,[^w11]
born in the clan of the Śākyas,
In your household, O Hero, I
was the leader, the lord of all
All of those women, endowed with
the virtues of beauty and grace,
in the home of the Śākyan Son,
they’re the same in pleasure and pain,[^w14]
fixed as the essence of beauty,
[her] eyes were the moon and the sun,
[In her] beak, mountain at world’s end,[^w22]
[she carried] a tree[^w23] with its roots.
the moon and the sun, Mount Meru,
and Śakra, [the king of the gods].
she preached the doctrine of merit;[^w26]
I worship your feet, Eyeful One.”
I’m also a master, Great Sage,
of the knowledge in others’ hearts.
In meaning and in the Teaching,
in your presence, O Great Hero.
the World-Lords, was well-seen by you;[^w28]
was for the sake of you, Great Sage.
O Sage, recall the good karma,
[that] merit was heaped up by me
for the sake of you, Great Hero.
for the sake of you, Great Hero.
I gave myself to be a wife,
I was not distressed about that,
for the sake of you, O Great Sage.
I gave myself to do service,
I was not distressed about that,
for the sake of you, O Great Sage.
I was not distressed about that,
for the sake of you, O Great Sage.
I have given you [all my] lives,
Great Sage, for your sake I do not[^w32]
conceal the things of a woman,
Wealth and grain have been given up,
fields and sons and daughters [as well]
have been given up, O Great Sage.
are given up beyond all count
for the sake of you, O Great Sage.
as alms to beggars, I give [that];
of diverse types, beyond all count,
for the sake of you, Great Hero.
for the sake of you, O Great Sage.
the Teaching for which[^w38] Buddha[^w39] strived.
By you [and] by me there was much
I performed a lot of service,
for the sake of you, O Great Sage;
while you sought the Buddha’s Teaching,[^w42]
the Leader of the World was born.
the road [on which] he is coming.
At that time there was a brahmin
He was making the road ready
for the All-Seer who was coming.
At that time I was a maiden,
known by the name of Sumittā.
I went up to that gathering.
With eight handfuls of blue lotus
in the midst of [all] the people
then I thought [like this to myself:]
“[this] life of mine is bearing fruit.”
At that time I saw [that] sage’s
heart was pleased in the Sambuddha.
I’m giving flowers to you, sage.[^w48]
There are five handfuls for you, sage;
Let there be success through[^w50] this [gift]
Famed One, Great Sage[^w53] who was coming.
[for that] sage with a lofty mind.
be exalted, that Sage So Great:[^w55]
through this karma she’ll be loving
for the sake of you, O great sage.[^w56]
she will be a loving woman,
so this one likewise will protect
[all] of the things that are wholesome.
Like a lion [freed] from a cage,
I lived behaving in that way
I brought pleasure to [my] mind when
that karma was well done [by me];
I was born in the Śākyan clan.
I have no fear from anything.
on what the Blessed One had said
within the harem of the king
and [one] who feels pleasure and pain,
a woman[^w61] who declares the facts,
Listen to my [words,] O great king:
listen to my [words], O great king:
Listen to my [words,] O great king:
listen to my words, O great king:
Listen to my [words,] O great king:
listen to my [words,] O great king:
There have been a million million
who were Chief Leaders of the World;
Listen to my [words,] O great king:
who were Leaders of the World [too.]
listen to my [words,] O great king:
listen to my [words,] O great king:
listen to my [words,] O great king:
listen to my [words,] O great king:
of those practiced in the teachings,[^w67]
in this world and in the other.
in this world and in the other.
When eight months[^w68] had not yet elapsed
Like the waves upon the ocean,
monastic robes and alms to eat,
was a very good thing for me.
[I have] done what the Buddha taught!
[I have] done what the Buddha taught!
the pure life [now] has been achieved,
for the merit of the Great Sage
all of my karma is destroyed:
I worship your feet, Eyeful One.”
Thus indeed Bhikkhunī Yasodharā spoke these verses.
The legend of Yasodharā Therī[^w71] is finished

notes.1: these first six verses appear in BJTS, but not PTS.
notes.3: reading satehi satassehi sā (BJTS) for satehi saha pañcchahi (“by five hundred,” PTS). As the subsequent three apadānas make clear, these authors believed that Yasodharā approached the Buddha accompanied by considerably more than 500 nuns.
notes.4: reading ettha with BJTS for PTS nāma (“indeed”)
notes.6: lit., “to/of the Teacher,” “give reverence to the Teacher”
notes.7: PTS khalitaŋ cche tavaŋ mayi, BJTS khalitaṃ cche mamaṃ tayi, both to be construed the same way
notes.10: “in the dispensation” may be governed by “all the assemblies” or, as I have it here, “doubt;” the grammar is ambiguous; the alternate reading would be “let doubt be cut off for all the/assemblies in th’ dispensation”
notes.12: reading itthi-y-aṅge (lit., “in the body of women”) with BJTS for PTS itthi atho (“and a woman who is established”)
notes.16: this verse does not appear in PTS, whereas PTS supplies (15) which does not appear in BJTS. The two verses are sufficiently different to warrant inclusion of both, though it creates some unevenness in the flow of the narrative here. The Pāli is: evamādīni vatvāna uppatitvāna ambaraṃ/iddhi anekā dassesi buddhānuññā yasodharā
notes.19: this verse does not appear here in BJTS, whereas BJTS supplies [974] which does not appear here in PTS. The two verses are sufficiently different to warrant inclusion of both, though it creates some unevenness in the flow of the narrative here. This verse does appear in BJTS below [1054], as in PTS, in the reduplication of Yasodharā’s apadāna as the apadāna of Eighteen Thousand Buddhist Nuns Headed Up by Yasodharā.
notes.20: cchakkavālaŋ samaŋ (BJTS cchakkavāḷasamaṃ) kāyaŋ, lit., “body the same as the ring surrounding the universe”
notes.21: or Uttarakuru “island” (dīpa). This verse presumes knowledge of the ancient Indian understanding of India (here jambudīpaŋ [BJTS °dīpo], “the Island of Rose-Apples”) as one of the four great islands or continents making up the whole world. It lies to the south, with the other three being north, east and west of India.
notes.22: lit., “in the ring surrounding the universe” (cchakkavālagiri°; BJTS cchakkavāḷagiri°)
notes.25: reading phullapadmena with BJTS for PTS phullapaccchchena (?)
notes.27: reading buddhānaṃ with BJTS (or PTS alt. Buddhāna) for PTS pubbānaŋ (former)
notes.28: saṅgaman te su-dassitaŋ allows for a wide range of meanings; here I follow the BJTS in a fairly modest one. The half-verse could be taken more provocatively to mean, e.g., “when the Buddhas were World-Lords (or “during the time of the former World-Lords”) meeting (or “intercourse”) with you was well seen [by me]”
notes.29: reading vārayitvā anāccharaṃ with BJTS for PTS pācchayantī anāvaraŋ (“burning/tormenting ?)
notes.30: abhabba-ṭṭhāne, the nine moral states or spheres of activity into which an arahant will not/cannot fall, D.iii.133 (and cf. D.iii.235 where only the first five appear as a set). This is Pāsādika Sutta, #29 of Dīghanikāya, section 26. The nine are: (1) cannot deliberately take the life of a living being (2) cannot steal (3) cannot have sexual intercourse (4) cannot deliberately lie (5) cannot hoard anything for his own indulgence (6) cannot act wrongly through attachments (7) cannot act wrongly through hatred (8) cannot act wrongly through folly (9) cannot act wrongly through fear
notes.31: reading sañcchattaṃ with BJTS (and PTS alt.) for PTS samattaŋ (“fulfilled” “completed”)
notes.32: reading °bhaṇḍe na gūhāmi with BJTS for PTS bhaṇḍena gūhāmi (“I conceal with a thing”)
notes.35: reading anubhuttaṃ with BJTS for PTS pariccchchattaŋ (“are sacrificed,” cf. PTS alt. anubhontaŋ)
notes.41: lit., “Sambuddha,” paralleling the usage in the previous verse
notes.42: reading gavesato buddhadhamme with BJTS for PTS gavesantā buddhadhammaŋ (“I, searching for the Buddha’s Teaching)
notes.45: reading cchīrānupari āsīnaṃ with BJTS for PTS cchirānugataŋ dassitaŋ (“associated for a long time, seen”)
notes.48: reading ise (voc.) with BJTS for PTS isiŋ (acc.)
notes.49: reading tayo with BJTS for PTS tato
notes.50: BJTS and PTS alt. read samā (“equal to”) for saha here,
notes.51: bodhanatthāya tavaŋ (PTS alt. tava); the phrase can also be translated, “for the sake of your knowing [me]”
notes.52: or, as above, “for the sake of knowing [me]”
notes.53: reading mahā-isiṃ (acc.) with BJTS for PTS mahā-isi (nom.)
notes.55: BJTS consigns this verse to an asterisked footnote, recognizing that it occurs in a number of its alternate recensions.
notes.56: BJTS agrees with PTS in presenting this as mahā-ise (voc.) but reference alternate readings mahā-isi (nom.), presumably troubled by the Buddha addressing Sumedha as “Great Sage”
notes.57: reading manāpā with BJTS for PTS manasā
notes.58: reading yathā…anurakkhanti sāmino with BJTS for PTS yathā…anurakkhati sāmi no (“as our master protects”)
notes.59: lit., “there is no agitation [to my mind]”
notes.60: This and the following 19 verses (20 verses total) are not included here in BJTS. vv. (62) and (63) do appear at BJTS [1092]-[1093]
notes.64: adhikāraŋ sadā mayhaŋ, lit., “my service is constant” “my service is daily”
notes.68: aṭṭhamāse, BJTS reads addhamāse (“half a month”)
notes.69: reading bahu ‘neke with BJTS for PTS buhun eke
notes.70: this and the following concluding verses do not appear here in PTS, and are unusual (though not unique) for Apadāna in which individual poems usually conclude with what I’ve dubbed the “concluding refrain” (vv. 85-87) [1023-1025]. Interestingly they (plus one more, also duplicated elsewhere) do appear, in the same unusual post-refrain position, below, as vv. 57-59 (plus 60) of apadāna #30, Eighteen Thousand Nuns with Yasodharā, and are also in this position in the BJTS version of that apadāna (vv. [1100-1102] plus [1103]).
notes.71: PTS omits Therī, which I supply from BJTS.
